title: The model
lede: An {{Ontology}} is the shape, not the content: which kinds of thing may exist, what may be said about each, and what may safely be inferred. Nine modules make up this one. **None of them is approved** — they live in `ontology/draft/` and move out one at a time, by a recorded human decision.

blocks.title: In one paragraph, for a reader who does not do this for a living
blocks.text: The model is written in {{OWL 2 RL}}, a standard language for describing kinds of thing and the rules between them. The **RL** part is a deliberate restriction: it trades expressive power for the guarantee that reasoning finishes quickly and predictably. Separately, {{SHACL}} states constraints that must hold before anything is published — think of {{OWL 2 RL}} as what the model *means* and {{SHACL}} as what it *refuses to let through*.

detail.text: The addressable shapes of the corpus. Maps onto upstream's page / chunk / provision / unit, NOT onto an idealised chapter-section-paragraph tree. Chapter and Paragraph appear in the roadmap's module list and are deliberately absent here. Some Manual subsections are bold text that was never marked up as a heading, so `heading_path` is a retrieval signal and a weak structural guarantee (Q-10). The addressable unit is `chunk_ref`, and a class named Paragraph would promise a structure the corpus does not carry.

What kind of thing is speaking, and with what force. This is the module CLAUDE.md rule 5 lives in. The Manual states the Registrar's practice; it does not bind the Registrar's discretion and it is not legislation. The distinction is carried here as a class disjointness rather than as a flag, because a flag can be dropped by a projection and a disjointness cannot be satisfied by an assertion that ignores it.

The concept layer, and the module with the largest declared-but-unpopulated part of the model. Every approved concept in `eval/gold/concepts.yaml` becomes a `tmk:LegalConcept`. Whether it is also one of the four subclasses below — GroundOfRefusal, LegalTest, RelevantFactor, Exception — depends on a signed record in `eval/gold/concept-types.yaml`, and on nothing else. Deciding that 'connotation' is a LegalTest rather than a RelevantFactor is a legal judgement this repo may not make (CLAUDE.md rule 1); what it may do is hold the answer somebody gives. The owner confirmed the four groups on 2026-09-08 (OQ-0001) and the container now exists (ADR-0071). Until a concept has a type record it stays a bare `tmk:LegalConcept`, and the count of unsorted concepts is reported by every build rather than defaulted away. A machine filling these would produce a taxonomy that reads as authoritative and was authored by nobody.

ADR-0011's field list as RDF, over PROV-O. The rule this module exists to make enforceable: an assertion that cannot say where it came from does not get published. Every approved relationship in the graph appears twice — once as a direct triple so SPARQL is natural, and once as a tmk:Assertion carrying the passage, the span, the hash, the reviewer and the date. A SHACL shape fails if the first exists without the second (ADR-0058). The field list is deliberately open (ADR-0041): Stage 2 has not run, so what a machine-generated candidate needs to carry is not yet known from evidence. What is here is what the approved records actually carry today.

The closed list of predicates extraction may propose. Derived from the 35 approved relationships in `eval/gold/relationships.yaml`: 14 distinct predicates, of which 6 are used exactly once. That last number is the one to read before treating this dictionary as settled — a term seen once is a term whose boundaries nobody has tested. Domain and range are `tmk:LegalMatter` throughout. The narrow types each predicate has actually been seen with are annotations and infer nothing; see tmk:LegalMatter in the legal-concepts module for why.
Declares no classes.

Who does what, and to what. Almost entirely **declared and unpopulated**, and that is the honest state: the approved set describes what the Manual says about section 43, not a process model of examination, and inventing one would be authoring practice. The role classes below are here for a specific reason. The reviewer's covering note (`review/returned/260826-expert-feedback.md`, HANDOFF Q17) named nine terms that need high-level definitions — Registrar, Delegate, Examiner, Decision Maker, Office Practice, Subject Matter Expert, Oppositions, Grounds for Rejection, Adverse Report — because the seed vocabulary was drawn from Part 29 alone and gives a narrow view of the roles. Declaring the classes empty is how that gap is made visible in the model rather than only in a document. Note also Q-28: a term's definition is usually not in a passage that cites anything, so ADR-0022's scope rule will not find these on its own.

**Entirely unpopulated, and the emptiest module in the draft on purpose.** The roadmap names it and the approved section 43 set says almost nothing about evidence: the pilot's material is about what a sign connotes, not about what an applicant files to establish something. Two records touch it — written permission overcoming a ground (GR-0039), information establishing that an applicant is the owner of a phoneword (GX-0010) — and neither is enough to model an evidence taxonomy from. Populating this is a Part 22/23 job (evidence of use under s 41), and Part 22 is explicitly out of the pilot scope draft. Left declared so the module list is complete and so nobody builds a second one.

Dates, currency and what this corpus cannot answer about time. The honest headline: **point-in-time questions are out of the pilot scope draft and the snapshot cannot support them.** There is no corpus-level version stamp (Q-05); the amendment history is the upstream repository's git history, and answering 'what guidance was current on «date»' properly needs a full-history clone, which is a different data strategy rather than a different query. CQ-0014 is marked out of scope on the strength of that line. What the module does carry is the currency mechanism that actually works: staleness by content hash. An assertion whose source hash no longer matches the pin is stale and returns to review. That is Stage 10's whole incremental mechanism and it needs no version stamp.

The Stage 0 measurement artefacts, in the graph rather than beside it. This module is not in the roadmap's module list and it earns its place: it is what lets a prohibited output be a node with edges instead of a paragraph in a YAML file. PU-0004 says that attributing the Manual's 'obvious, direct and immediate' formulation to the Act is prohibited and that the error is structurally detectable. It is only structurally detectable if the prohibition, the question it attaches to, and the passages involved are all in the same graph. Here they are, and `shapes/prohibited-use.ttl` reads them.

blocks.text:
### The predicates

A {{Predicate}} is the middle of a statement — *this passage **states** that concept*. The list is **generated** from the relationships an expert approved, and a test compares the file against a regeneration. That is deliberate: a hand-written list of allowed relationships would be an agent choosing the vocabulary of the domain. To add one, have a reviewer approve a relationship that uses it.

rows.name: `AuthoredAssertion`
rows.label: Authored assertion
rows.search: AuthoredAssertion Authored assertion An assertion a machine wrote and no expert has validated (ADR-0079, ADR-0080). Deliberately NOT a subclass of tmk:ApprovedAssertion and deliberately not in the approved named graph. It is the same shape as one — same subject, predicate, object, passage, span and hash — and differs in exactly the fact that matters: nobody signed it. A query written against tmk:ApprovedAssertion therefore cannot pick one of these up by accident, which is the whole point of giving it its own class rather than a flag. It carries tmk:reviewStatus "unreviewed" and never "approved": approval moves a record to eval/gold/ through tmk-transcribe, and a record that has moved is rebuilt as a tmk:ApprovedAssertion on the next build (ADR-0086).

So the edge is a node: it carries how it was found and how certain that was, and `tmk:citesProvision` exists beside it only as a convenience for queries that genuinely do not care.

blocks.note: Counted over the approved graph only — the one this repository commits. The source graph, which is rebuilt rather than stored, populates several more (passages, citations, decisions); the ontology report counts those. An empty class is a slot waiting for content, not a bug: the four that matter most — ground of refusal, legal test, relevant factor, exception — are empty because sorting the 52 legal ideas into them is a legal judgement.
